messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
# Rajesh

Rajesh was forty-three when his daughter Priya fell ill. She had complained of a sore throat one Tuesday morning, nothing unusual for a child heading into autumn, but by Thursday her fever had climbed past 104 degrees and she lay in the pediatric ward of County General, her small body tethered to machines he did not fully understand. The doctors spoke of meningitis, of a lumbar puncture, of antibiotics. Rajesh, who had spent twenty years defusing ordnance—who had learned to steady his hands while kneeling beside a device that could unmake him in microseconds—found himself unable to steady anything. He watched the neurologist approach with a needle longer than any he had ever seen, watched Priya's face contort as they held her still, and something fractured inside him that he had kept intact through decades of controlled breathing and compartmentalization. For six days she hovered between recovery and catastrophe. When she finally turned the corner, when the fever broke and the antibiotics began to work, Rajesh had already been remade by the helplessness of those hours—by the knowledge that his vigilance, his years of training, his ability to read danger and neutralize it, had meant nothing here. A child's body was not a bomb. You could not defuse illness.

Fifteen years have passed. Priya is healthy now, a college student studying engineering. But Rajesh, at fifty-eight, finds himself trapped in a vigilance that has never truly loosened. He lies awake most nights, his mind refusing to settle into sleep, convinced that some catastrophe is imminent—not just for Priya, but for his wife Meera, for anyone he loves. He is certain that his inability to protect them, demonstrated so thoroughly in that hospital room, means he is fundamentally weak, that he has failed at the most basic requirement of being a man and a father. When he catches himself scanning for threats in ordinary moments—cataloguing exits, listening for the sound of an ambulance—he becomes convinced that his mind is fracturing, that he is losing his grip on reality. These thoughts terrify him more than the original trauma.

Three months ago, Meera developed a routine dental infection. When she mentioned needing to see a specialist, Rajesh felt his chest tighten. The thought of any medical setting, any hospital, sent him spiraling. He declined to accompany her, claiming work obligations, but the real reason was far more shameful: the moment he imagined stepping through those doors again, smelling that particular antiseptic—that sharp, chemical smell that had soaked into his clothes during Priya's hospitalization—his body responded as though the threat were immediate and present. His heart would race, his palms would sweat, and suddenly he was not fifty-eight years old in 2024; he was in that pediatric ward, watching his daughter in agony. The memory came without warning, complete and sensory, as if every nerve ending in his body was reliving that moment. He could see the needle approaching Priya's spine, could hear her crying, could feel the impotence that had hollowed him out. Each time the antiseptic smell returned—in a doctor's office, in a pharmacy—it arrived with a thought that felt indistinguishable from truth: he was fundamentally incapable of protecting anyone who mattered. The smell did not merely trigger the memory; it told him something damning about himself.

These intrusions have begun to reshape his life in ways he cannot control. Last month, his team at the bomb disposal unit was called to a school where a suspicious package had been found. Rajesh, who had trained for this work his entire career, found himself unable to focus on the technical problem in front of him. A group of children had been evacuated to a nearby playground, and their presence—their smallness, their vulnerability—triggered the same cascade of memory and dread that the hospital smell had. He saw Priya in every one of them. The sight of those children on the playground crystallized something he had been avoiding: he was a man who could not be trusted with what he loved most. Their presence was evidence of his weakness. His hands shook as he worked. His supervisor noticed. Since then, Rajesh has begun to avoid the school calls, volunteering for other assignments, making excuses. His reputation, built over decades, is beginning to crack. At home, he finds himself unable to be in the same room when his grandniece visits; he makes reasons to work late, to stay in the garage. Meera has started to ask questions, hurt and confused by his distance from family, and Rajesh cannot explain to her that being around children now feels like standing at the edge of a precipice—that their presence is a reminder of everything he cannot protect, everything he failed to prevent. Every time his grandniece's laugh drifted through the house, it reinforced what had become certainty: he was a failure as a protector, a man unfit for the people who depended on him.

The worst part is the conviction, which has grown harder to shake with each passing week, that his reactions prove something fundamentally broken inside him. A strong man would have moved past this. A capable man would not be haunted by a trauma that happened fifteen years ago, when his daughter survived. He lies awake at three in the morning, his mind cycling through the same thoughts: he is weak, he is going mad, he cannot stop bad things from happening. And because he believes these things about himself, he finds himself more alert, more vigilant, more certain that danger is always seconds away. The vigilance feeds the belief, which feeds the memory, which feeds the conviction that he is coming apart at the seams.

Last week, Rajesh finally made an appointment. He told Meera only that he was having trouble sleeping, but the truth is more complicated and more frightening: he is running out of room inside himself to contain what happened. He is afraid that if he does not find help soon, he will lose not just his career but his family—that the distance he has created between himself and the people he loves will become permanent, and he will have failed them again.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: Triggers (antiseptic smell, children on playground) and Negative Appraisals (he is fundamentally incapable, he is a failure, he is weak) appear throughout the vignette but no single paragraph clearly conveys that a trigger directly drives or leads to a negative appraisal—the causal chain is mediated through Memory and Threat rather than direct causation.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: Negative Appraisals (beliefs about his weakness and failure) do not causally drive or generate new triggers; instead, the vignette shows appraisals reinforcing existing threat responses and vigilance cycles rather than producing triggering stimuli themselves.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The memory came without warning, complete and sensory, as if every nerve ending in his body was reliving that moment. He could see the needle approaching Priya's spine, could hear her crying, could feel the impotence that had hollowed him out. Each time the antiseptic smell returned—in a doctor's office, in a pharmacy—it arrived with a thought that felt indistinguishable from truth: he was fundamentally incapable of protecting anyone who mattered.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The smell did not merely trigger the memory; it told him something damning about himself. Each exposure to that sharp, chemical scent carried with it the quiet certainty that he was weak, that he had failed at the most basic requirement of being a father, and that this failure was not temporary but constitutive—woven into who he was.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Last month, his team at the bomb disposal unit was called to a school where a suspicious package had been found. Rajesh, who had trained for this work his entire career, found himself unable to focus on the technical problem in front of him. A group of children had been evacuated to a nearby playground, and their presence—their smallness, their vulnerability—triggered the same cascade of memory and dread that the hospital smell had.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The sight of those children on the playground crystallized something he had been avoiding: he was a man who could not be trusted with what he loved most. Once he had settled into the conviction that he was fundamentally incapable of protecting those who depended on him, almost any reminder of vulnerability—a child's laugh, a small hand, the sight of a playground—became a fresh confirmation of that terrible truth, each one sharpening the certainty that danger was always seconds away.
<<<END>>>
